Site info:
In 1959 Phil C. Orr discovered two human femora
partially exposed in sediments 11 m deep in the arroyo wall
of Arlington Canyon. In 1960 after convening a team of
scholars from several scientific disciplines to examine the
archaeological and stratigraphic context of this find, an irregular
block of earth (60 cm x 40 cm x 33 cm) was removed
containing the bones. These samples are from that block of earth.
Museum/Institution: Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History
Contact info: 2559 Puesta del Sol Rd., Santa Barbara, CA 93105 - 001 (805) 682-4711

Site info: Feature 1 is a well preserved midpassage dwelling. Prior to excavation the midpassage was hidden in Mountain Avens, willow, grasses, Cinquefoil (Potentilla chamissonis) and mosses, and the stones were covered by the red leichen Alloplaga elegans. In the midpassage there is a hearth box set between the two parallel rows of vertically standing flagstones, that makes up the walls in the midpassage itself. However, prior to excavation many of the originally vertically placed stones had tilted. The hearth box measures 50 by 60 cm, and the five cm wide flagstones were raised five to twelve cm above the surrounding gravel surface. Smaller fist sized stones are jammed on the outside of the parallel rows of vertically placed flagstones and in the front part of the feature, there is a large flagstone. Feature 1 was excavated in 1966, revealing a total of 120 artefacts (L1.8742-8788) including two bone needles and three pieces of worked bone. The remainder 115 artefacts are stone tools or debitage according to the table below. In Knuths publications Feature I is often depicted as a typical midpassage structure (Knuth 1967). However as can be seen in “Reports from the Musk-Ox Way” (Knuth 1984:60-61) the Feature is reconstructed in the appearance with vertically standing flagstones. The exact situation of the bonematerial associated with fearyre 1 is not known, but most of the muskox bones are believed to have been collected from the midden area in front of the ruin.

Depositional environment: Sampling occurred roughly 155 meters to the NW from WHSA Locality 2 (see Bennett et al. 2021 - https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abg7586). WHSA Locality 2 is located on the eastern side of Alkali Flat on a shallow (<6 m) erosional scarp formed between the current playa and the White Sands gypsum dune field. A sedimentary sequence exposed by trenching consists of 1.25 m of lacustrine clays and silts intercalated with thinly bedded gypsiferous and siliciclastic sands, silts, and clays, which represent a transition from a lacustrine ecosystem to an alluvial regime in response to changing hydroclimate conditions during the late Pleistocene. Endocarps of ditch grass (Ruppia cirrhosa) occur as discontinuous layers throughout the sequence.
Site info: This site is adjacent a pre-Clovis site of human foorprints dated to 23 kya

Depositional environment: Sampling occurred roughly 155 meters to the NW from WHSA Locality 2 (see Bennett et al. 2021 - https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abg7586). WHSA Locality 2 is located on the eastern side of Alkali Flat on a shallow (<6 m) erosional scarp formed between the current playa and the White Sands gypsum dune field. A sedimentary sequence exposed by trenching consists of 1.25 m of lacustrine clays and silts intercalated with thinly bedded gypsiferous and siliciclastic sands, silts, and clays, which represent a transition from a lacustrine ecosystem to an alluvial regime in response to changing hydroclimate conditions during the late Pleistocene. Endocarps of ditch grass (Ruppia cirrhosa) occur as discontinuous layers throughout the sequence.
Site info: This site is adjacent a pre-Clovis site of human foorprints dated to 23 kya

Field code=S1R1-001a; Sampling date: 19 June 2019, during daytime, sunny weather

Sampling locality: Meadow at approximately 200 meters height up on the mountain behind the Grønnedal naval base (several photos). This mountain is part of the Grønnedal-Íka igneous complex.

Sampling description: 
Underlying bedrock is syenite (silica-undersaturated rock type). Sampling of soil was carried out at five different positions, listed on the field sheet. We tried to take the samples at 5-10 m distance to each other. The whole meadow, as also seen on the photos, was just grasses and moss. No shrubbery, bushes etc.

Field code=S3R1-003a; Sampling date: 21 June 2019, just before midnight, partly cloudy but no precipitation

Sampling locality: Samples are taken around a norse ruin (stable) on the northern shore of Ikka Fjord (see drone image of the area, including close-up of the ruin). 

Sampling description: 
Underlying bedrock is nepheline syenite and possibly carbonatite (calcite-rich rock type), again on top of thick scree material. There were also several boulders cropping up. Sample no. 3 is taken inside the ruin walls. According to archeological descriptions of this ruin, it´s supposed to have been a stable for the animals. The soil within the stable area was very different from all other soil samples we took. It appeared to be more organic rich and reddish in colour.

Sample type: Ca. 2 L bag sample (subsampled in 20 ml tubes)
Depositional environment: Sample collected from freshly exposed cut in permafrost at a placer gold mine. Sampled sediment is organic-rich silt interbed within crudely-bedded quartz-rich coarse gravels. Well-preserved wood fragments are common in the sampled bed.
Contact info: 1-26 Earth Sciences Bldg/Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences/Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, T6G 2E3/tel 780-492-8171/email areyes@ualberta.ca
References: Sample collected from freshly exposed cut in permafrost at a placer gold mine. Sampled sediment is organic-rich silt interbed within crudely-bedded quartz-rich coarse gravels. Well-preserved wood fragments are common in the sampled bed.
Notes: Age is based on identification of the unit as the White Channel Gravel. The lower White Channel Gravel has pollen consistent with a middle Pliocene age, and has a paleomagnetic reversal from reversed to normal polarity that is probably associated with Gilbert-Gauss chron transition at ~3.6 Ma. The age of the upper White Channel must be older than 2.64 Ma based on cosmogenic burial dates on the overlying Klondike Gravel. Dated tephra beds within the upper White Channel Gravel date to ~3.3-2.6 Ma. The sampled bed was not deposited during a time of permafrost. Permafrost likely first affected the site ~2.6 Ma, with deep thaw during Early Pleistocene interglacials and possible permafrost persistence through most Middle and Late Pleistocene interglacials.
